newsitem.title: New zealand: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 14.

text.p: A joint computer project of the New Zealand and Australian national libraries, which has already cost the National Library almost NZ$9 million, has in effect been abandoned. A spokeswoman for Wyatt Creech, the misiter responsible for the National Library, was unable to say on Monday how much the library would get back of the $8.8 million it spent before the decision was made not to go ahead. The national document information system project (NDIS) failed because of software problems. Page 1.

Tougher bail laws, which the government has agreed to consider, might not be desirable, Justice Minister Doug Graham has said. Under its coalition agreement, the government has agreed to consider giving police the power to require three days' notice of a defendant's intention to apply for bail and a copy of the grounds under which bail is sought. Graham said the proposal had been raised by Rana Waitai, a NZ First MP and former Gisborne police commander. Page 2.

Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare plans to fight for the survival of Maori television station Aotearoa Television Network. The future of the pilot Maori television station is under a cloud, and 20 of its 92 staff will lose their jobs in a bid to keep the station on air. The station has been forced to axe jobs because funding from the Maori broadcasting funding agency, Te Mangai Paho, ends in February. Page 2.

Labour Maori affairs spokesman Dover Samuels on Monday slated Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare for refusing to issue post-election briefing papers on Maori affairs. Samuels said Henare was the only minister to refuse Labour's request for briefing papers. "What's he trying to hide? Even Treasury and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade -- usually the most secretive of government agencies -- have made pubic releases of their briefing papers," Samuels said. Page 2.

The success of the law that made teacher registration compulsory again had prompted plans to promote a member's bill to abolish teacher salary bulk-funding, Labour education spokesman Trevor Mallard said. The registration law was working successfully so far, with double the number of applications than normal for this time of year, he said. Page 2.

MetService forecasts of cyclones Drena and Fergus had helped reduce damage from flooding around New Zealand, the Insurance Council said on Monday. The early warnings had allowed holiday makers, homeowners and local authorities to be better prepared
for the storms, preventing further damage from flooding, council spokeswoman Catherine Beard said. Page 6.

The thriving export trade of boatbuilders is under threat from the high Kiwi dollar. The Marine Export Group of the New Zealand said on Monday that the industry had seen huge growth in recent years, jumping from $82 million in 1994 to $159 million last year. But boatbuilders said buyers needed a signigicant price advantage to make up for transportation costs and the cost of flying to New Zealand to take part in the building process. Page 13.

Inflation data due on Friday should answer the question of whether last week's fall in interest rates was sustainable but not larger questions about economic growth, economists said on Monday. Ninety-day bank bill yields fell to 7.5 percent last week as the currency rose to an eight-year high of 68.36 on its Trade-Weighted Index. Ninety-day bank bills closed on Monday at 7.53 percent and the Trade-Weighted Index closed at 68.0 after a sell-off in the United States market on Friday stifled trade. Page 13.
